lcontroversial_reading.cultural_notes_en:
Defending a controversial reading is the Königsdisziplin of C2 Germanistik — it's what separates doctoral students from those at the Habilitation level. (1) STEELMANNING vs STRAWMANNING: the Anglophone distinction between 'steelmanning' (reconstructing the opposing position in its strongest form) and 'strawmanning' (deforming it and fighting the caricature). The C2 critic only steelmans. Weakest form of defence: 'Others say X, that's wrong.' Strongest form: 'The strongest variant of the opposing position I know is X (proponent Y, argument Z) — even against that variant, the following can be said...'. (2) DIFFERENTIATED RECOGNITION: a successful defence of a controversial reading doesn't claim 'my reading is right'. Instead: 'my reading opens up a perspective that hasn't been systematically pursued yet'. That modesty gesture isn't false modesty — it's methodologically honest. Two readings can be productive at the same time. (3) MARKING THE SCOPE: a controversial reading is stronger when its limits are stated explicitly. 'My reading carries for X, not for Y' defends itself better than 'My reading explains everything'.

Different from Vietnam: Vietnamese criticism tends toward a 'right/wrong' framework. In German C2 it's 'productive/unproductive' — multiple readings can coexist. The doctoral supervisor will check: 'Does your reading make the other reading obsolete — or supplement it?' If you claim obsolescence, the evidence bar is very high.

One important detail: defence is not polemic. Polemic (sharp criticism in an aggressive tone) has its own tradition in the German feuilleton (Karl Kraus, Reich-Ranicki). But scholarly defence is not polemic — it's substantive and sober. Personalising it ('Vaget didn't understand this') is a reliable sign of a weak argument.

On reading Mann 'against the grain': a classic research example is Lukács vs Adorno on Mann. Lukács read Mann as a progressive bourgeois realist. Adorno (in 'Versuch über Wagner' and in 'Aesthetic Theory') read Mann as a self-critic of the bourgeoisie. Both readings are productive, both controversial in their day against bourgeois Mann-worship. A C2 analyst can use these readings as models.

On Bachmann 'against the grain': feminist Bachmann scholarship positioned itself against the bourgeois Bachmann veneration of the 1960s, which read her as a 'tragic poet'. The feminist reading: Bachmann as an analytic critic of patriarchal structures — controversial but now well established (Weigel, Stephan, Anna Tanneberger).

On Goethe 'against the grain': postcolonial readings of the 'Divan' are controversial — against Goethe-worship as 'congenial Persian intermediary'. Here scope has to be marked clearly: the postcolonial reading carries for certain aspects (the construction of 'the Orient'), not for others (the formal adaptation of the Hafis-Ghasel).

On 'defence economy': in oral defence (Disputation, Habilitation, conference) you get about 5 minutes per objection. Economical argument: 1 sentence acknowledging the objection → 2 sentences with the strongest variant of the opposing position → 2 sentences with your own answer → 1 sentence marking the scope. Total: 6 sentences, roughly 90 seconds.

Core further reading (argumentation theory):
- Stephen Toulmin, 'The Uses of Argument' (1958)
- Frans van Eemeren, 'Strategic Maneuvering in Argumentative Discourse'
- Theodor W. Adorno, 'Versuch über Wagner' — model of a controversial reading
- Georg Lukács, 'Thomas Mann' (1949) — controversial reading from within the bourgeois tradition
- Sigrid Weigel, 'Die Stimme der Medusa' — model for a gender-critical defence
lcontroversial_reading.tip_advice_en:
C2 defence of a controversial reading in five steps:
1. STEELMANNING. Reconstruct the strongest variant of the opposing position. Who is the leading dissenting voice? Which argument is the strongest? Prepare it in full.
2. ACKNOWLEDGMENT. Signal that you take the opposing position seriously — not condescendingly, not ironically.
3. ARGUMENT. Put your answer in sober, substantive terms — no polemic, no personalisation.
4. SCOPE-MARKING. State what your reading carries for and what it doesn't. This strengthens, it does not weaken.
5. SELF-REFLECTION. Where does your argument run out? Where does productive tension remain? Acknowledge it.

C2 phrasing for defending a controversial reading:
- 'Eine kontroverse Lektüre lässt sich nicht durch Behauptung verteidigen, sondern allein durch eine Argumentation, die ihre Voraussetzungen offenlegt' (a controversial reading can't be defended by assertion, only by an argument that lays its premises open)
- 'Wer Mann gegen den Strich liest, muss diese Lesart gegen den hermeneutischen Konsens verteidigen' (reading Mann against the grain means having to defend that reading against the hermeneutic consensus)
- 'Die Verteidigung gelingt nicht als Abwehr, sondern als sorgfältige Aufnahme der Einwände' (defence succeeds not as parrying but as careful uptake of the objections)
- 'Wer den Gegenstandpunkt nicht in seiner stärksten Form rekonstruiert, hat seinen eigenen nicht verstanden' (anyone who doesn't reconstruct the opposing position in its strongest form hasn't understood their own)
- 'Ihre Lesart ist nicht ‚richtiger', sondern eröffnet eine bislang nicht systematisch verfolgte Perspektive' (your reading is not 'more correct' — it opens up a perspective that hasn't been systematically pursued)
- 'Wo die Argumentation erschöpft ist, beginnt die kritische Selbstreflexion' (where the argument runs out, critical self-reflection begins)

The steelmanning move:
- 'Die stärkste mir bekannte Variante der Gegenposition stammt von [Name] und argumentiert wie folgt: [stated in full strength]. Selbst gegen diese Variante lässt sich folgendes anführen: [your reply]' (the strongest variant of the opposing position I know comes from [name] and argues as follows: [state in full strength]. Even against that variant, the following can be said: [your reply])

The differentiated-recognition move:
- 'Die etablierte Lesart trägt für X — meine Lesart trägt für Y. Beide Lesarten konkurrieren nicht um eine ‚richtige' Auslegung, sondern öffnen unterschiedliche Aspektfelder' (the established reading carries for X; mine carries for Y. The two readings aren't competing for a 'correct' interpretation — they open different fields of aspects)

Scope-marking:
- 'Meine Lesart trägt nicht für die formalen Aspekte — sie konzentriert sich auf die ideologische Dimension' (my reading doesn't carry for the formal aspects — it focuses on the ideological dimension)
- 'Diese Argumentation hat ihre Grenzen: sie funktioniert für Werk X, weniger für Werk Y' (this argument has its limits: it works for work X, less for work Y)

The self-reflection move:
- 'Wo erschöpft sich diese Argumentation? An der Stelle, an der [concrete example]. Hier muss eine ergänzende Perspektive einsetzen' (where does this argument run out? At the point where [concrete example]. A complementary perspective has to come in here)
- 'Auch eine kontroverse Lektüre weiß um ihre Grenzen, ohne sich deshalb zurückzunehmen' (even a controversial reading knows its limits without retreating because of them)

When polemic threatens:
- 'Erlauben Sie mir, sachlich zu antworten' (allow me to answer in substantive terms)
- 'Ich möchte den persönlichen Aspekt zurückstellen und auf das Argument fokussieren' (I'd like to set the personal aspect aside and focus on the argument)

When the consensus is strong:
- 'Der hermeneutische Konsens ist nicht Wahrheit, sondern Forschungsmehrheit — eine Differenz, die für die Argumentation entscheidend ist' (the hermeneutic consensus is not truth but a scholarly majority — a distinction that's decisive for the argument)

Never do this:
- 'X didn't understand it' (personalisation, weak argument)
- 'This criticism is unjustified' (assertion instead of argument)
- Strawmanning the opposing position
- 'My reading is the only correct one' (anti-pluralistic, methodologically sloppy)
- Polemic without substantive content

Last tip: before every defence, write a one-page 'steelmanning memo' — the strongest opposing position in full form. If you can't reconstruct that form convincingly, your own position isn't ready yet.
lcontroversial_reading.register_notes_en: C2 defence of a controversial reading: steelmanning is required — reconstruct the opposing position in its strongest form. Five-step structure: steelmanning → acknowledgment → argument → scope-marking → self-reflection. Konjunktiv I for indirect quotation: 'Vaget zufolge sei das Verfallsschema als bürgerliche Selbstkritik zu lesen'. Funktionsverbgefüge: 'in voller Stärke rekonstruieren' (reconstruct in full strength), 'in den Blick nehmen' (bring into focus), 'zur Geltung bringen' (bring into force). Differentiated-recognition formula: 'Your reading is not ‚more correct' — it opens up a perspective that hasn't been systematically pursued.' Avoid 'X didn't understand' (personalisation); avoid 'my reading is the only correct one' (anti-pluralistic). Polemic ≠ scholarly defence — substantive and sober, not aggressive. On the consensus claim: 'The hermeneutic consensus is not truth, it's a scholarly majority.' Ideal Disputation answer in six sentences: 1 acknowledgment + 2 steelmanning + 2 your answer + 1 scope — about 90 seconds.

idiom_glosses_en.example_en: Anyone who stands up to the hermeneutic consensus has to double-check their argument.

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: to turn the tables, to reverse the situation (standardsprachlich)
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: My argument turns the tables: the decay-narrative itself is the bourgeois gesture Mann is staging.

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: to be on solid ground, to have a firm basis (standardsprachlich)
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: A controversial reading has to stand on solid ground — otherwise it breaks under the first objection.

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: to take your opponent seriously, to respect the opposing position (standardsprachlich)
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: Steelmanning means taking your opponent so seriously that you formulate their best objection yourself — before they raise it.

larts_kunstkritik.cultural_notes_en:
KUNSTKRITIK IN THE GERMAN TRADITION:

(1) LESSING (1729-1781): 'Laokoon, or On the Limits of Painting and Poetry' (1766) — drew a sharp line between bildende Kunst (visual art, spatial, simultaneous) and Dichtung (poetry, temporal, successive). The aftershock is still felt today: a critique of a painting shouldn't 'tell a story' (the narrative fallacy).

(2) GOETHE: 'Über Kunst und Altertum' (1816-1832) — Goethe's journal that shaped art criticism as a literary genre. His 'Theory of Colours' (Farbenlehre, 1810) analysed the optics and psychology of colour.

(3) BEUYS (1921-1986): the 'expanded concept of art' — ''Every human being is an artist.'' Social sculpture: society as a total work of art in which everyone takes part in shaping form. Documenta, Kunstakademie Düsseldorf.

(4) RICHTER (1932-): painting after photography. The blur (Verwischung) as a critique of the image's claim to truth. 'Atlas' — his vast photographic archive.

(5) THE FEUILLETON TRADITION: FAZ (Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung), SZ (Süddeutsche Zeitung), Die Zeit — the cultural feuilleton is an institution. A print art review still carries more weight in Germany than in the Anglo-American press.

(6) DOCUMENTA (Kassel, every five years): the most important contemporary art exhibition in the world. Each Documenta generates thousands of pages of German-language Kunstkritik. A C2 student should read at least one Documenta catalogue raisonné.

(7) NOTE FOR ENGLISH-SPEAKING LEARNERS: German Kunstkritik leans heavily on nominalisation (Substantivierung): 'das In-Beziehung-Setzen', 'das Sich-Einlassen auf…'. This is a hallmark of German academic prose — don't try to translate it back into the verb-driven style of English journalism.
larts_kunstkritik.tip_advice_en:
STRUCTURE OF A C2 FEUILLETON ART REVIEW (2,500-4,000 characters):

1. EINSTIEG (2-3 sentences): open with a concrete observation — a colour, a material, a curatorial gesture. Never 'The exhibition shows works by…'.
- 'Already in the first room your step falters: a monochrome grey that, on closer inspection, fractures into dozens of shades.'

2. BESCHREIBUNG (25%): precise, objective description. German readers expect Präzision: material, technique, dimensions. 'Oil on canvas, 200 × 300 cm' is non-negotiable.

3. KONTEXTUALISIERUNG (20%): place the work within the artist's œuvre and within art history — briefly. Germans hate empty name-dropping.

4. DEUTUNG (40%): interpretation. The heart of the piece. Two or three angles:
- Formal: how does the material act on the viewer?
- Historical: which tradition does the work stand in?
- Social: what does the work say about our present?
Each angle needs a topic sentence: 'The work can be read as a comment on…'

5. URTEIL (15%): a reasoned verdict. Germans want a clear judgement, argued for. 'Gelungen' / 'weniger überzeugend' — and why.

USEFUL PHRASES:
- 'Das Werk gibt zu denken, dass…' (the work makes one think that…)
- 'In der Tradition von X stehend, bricht das Werk doch zugleich mit…' (standing in the tradition of X, the work nevertheless breaks with…)
- 'Die Materialentscheidung ist hier alles andere als beliebig.' (the choice of material here is anything but arbitrary.)
- 'Gerade im Scheitern des Anspruchs liegt die eigentliche Aussage.' (the real statement lies precisely in the failure of the claim.)

AVOID:
- Schwärmerei (gushing): German readers distrust writers who sound 'enthralled'.
- Biographism: the artist's private life is no substitute for Werkbeschreibung.
- Unbelegte Behauptungen (unsupported claims): every assertion must be anchored in the work itself.
larts_kunstkritik.register_notes_en:
C2 GERMAN KUNSTKRITIK — register markers:

KONJUNKTIV I for indirect speech: 'Richter himself says his painting is not a statement, but a questioning.' ('Richter selbst sagt, seine Malerei sei kein Statement, sondern ein Befragen.')
KONJUNKTIV II for counterfactuals: 'Had the jury hung the work differently, its spatial dimension would have become clearer.'

NOMINALSTIL: instead of 'the artist paints in order to show', write 'the painterly procedure serves to render visible…' ('das malerische Verfahren dient der Sichtbarmachung von…').

KOMPOSITA (compound nouns): a German speciality — Bildsprache, Materialgerechtigkeit, Wahrnehmungsbedingungen, Ausstellungsdispositiv. Don't be afraid to coin new compounds as long as they're transparent.

PASSIVE: very common in German academic writing: 'The work is read as a comment on consumer culture.'

MAN: the impersonal subject is everywhere: 'Man könnte einwenden, dass…' ('One could object that…'), 'Man sieht sich konfrontiert mit…' ('One finds oneself confronted with…').

FUNKTIONSVERBGEFÜGE (light-verb constructions): 'zur Anwendung kommen' (to be applied), 'in den Blick nehmen' (to bring into focus), 'zur Diskussion stellen' (to put up for discussion).

AVOID:
- 'Ich finde das Werk schön' → too subjective.
- Colloquialisms: 'toll', 'super', 'krass'.
- Too many Anglicisms: 'Das Statement des Künstlers' → 'Die Aussage des Künstlers' where possible.
- Unsupported claims: if you say 'the work critiques capitalism', you must show HOW (material, form, exhibition context).

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: To catch the eye immediately — used when describing what hits you on entering an exhibition.
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: The first thing that catches the eye is the monstrous chandelier — it's made of used tampons.

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: To give one pause for thought — formal, polite; used when a work refuses easy answers.
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: The work gives one pause for thought precisely because it resists any quick reading.

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: To realise / put into a work — formal, elevated register (gehoben).
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: What the artist sketches out theoretically he carries through consistently in this installation.

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: To put it precisely / nail it — used when praising an artist or a critic for hitting the mark.
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: This work nails the unease of the present moment.

larts_filmkritik.cultural_notes_en:
FILMKRITIK IN THE GERMAN TRADITION:

(1) KRACAUER (1889-1966): 'From Caligari to Hitler' (1947) — read Weimar cinema as the psychological pre-history of National Socialism. 'Theory of Film' (1960): cinema as the 'redemption of physical reality'.

(2) FASSBINDER (1945-1982): Neuer Deutscher Film. Melodrama as social critique. Heavily influenced by Douglas Sirk (the German-born Hollywood director). 'The Marriage of Maria Braun', 'Ali: Fear Eats the Soul' (Angst essen Seele auf).

(3) THE BERLIN SCHOOL: Christian Petzold, Maren Ade, Angela Schanelec, Thomas Arslan — the post-Wall generation. A new realism: no psychology, no explanation, only precise observation.

(4) HANEKE (Austrian, but writes in German): 'Caché', 'The White Ribbon', 'Amour' — cinema as an ethical interrogation of the viewer. Violence isn't shown, it's structured in the off-screen.

(5) BERLINALE: the Berlin International Film Festival — one of the Big Three (with Cannes and Venice). Heavily politicised (the Golden Bear often carries political weight).

(6) FILM CRITICISM IN THE PRESS: unlike the French tradition, German film criticism pays less attention to mise en scène and more to content / politics / society. FAZ, SZ, Die Zeit, taz, Der Spiegel each maintain their own film-criticism voice.

(7) NOTE FOR ENGLISH-SPEAKING LEARNERS: German Filmkritik leans on dense compound adjectives — 'gesellschaftskritisch' (society-critiquing), 'sozialrealistisch' (social-realist), 'kammerspielartig' (chamber-play-like). These have no one-word English equivalents and usually need a phrase to unpack.
larts_filmkritik.tip_advice_en:
STRUCTURE OF A FEUILLETON FILM REVIEW (3,000-5,000 characters):

1. VORSPANN (one sentence): the opening must cut — a single image, a sound, a paradox.

2. MINIMALE INHALTSANGABE (10%): the bare minimum plot summary. No spoilers.

3. FILMISCHE ANALYSE (50%) — the layers:
- Bildästhetik: camerawork, framing, light, colour.
- Montage: editing rhythm, ellipses, parallel cutting.
- Sound: music, noise, silence, voice-over.
- Schauspielführung: bodies, gesture, delivery.

4. EINORDNUNG (25%): place the film in the director's filmography, in its current of cinema, in its political and social moment.

5. FAZIT (15%): a clear verdict. German readers hate fence-sitting reviews.

USEFUL PHRASES:
- 'Der Film handelt nicht von…, sondern er handelt durch…' (the film isn't about…, it acts through…)
- 'Die Kamera ist hier keine Beobachterin, sondern eine Komplizin.' (the camera here isn't an observer, it's an accomplice.)
- 'Der Schnitt setzt weniger auf Kontinuität als auf Reibung.' (the editing relies less on continuity than on friction.)

AVOID:
- Nacherzählung (retelling the plot) — a Filmkritik isn't a synopsis.
- Betroffenheitsgestus ('this film moved me deeply') — too subjective for a German broadsheet.
- Blanket verdicts ('a masterpiece') without justification.
larts_filmkritik.register_notes_en:
C2 GERMAN FILMKRITIK:

PRÄSENS for description of what's on screen: 'The film begins with…', 'The camera follows…'
PERFEKT for commentary on directorial choices: 'The director has gone for an unusual framing here.'
KONJUNKTIV II for criticism: 'It would have been better to cut the scene shorter.'

PASSIVE: 'The film is carried by…', 'The tension is generated not by plot but by glances.'

PRECISE ADJECTIVES (not empty ones):
- 'sperrig' (difficult, resisting easy reception)
- 'spröde' (dry, refusing to flatter the viewer)
- 'lakonisch' (laconic, sparse dialogue)
- 'unterkühlt' (chilled below normal — emotionally restrained)

TECHNICAL PRECISION:
- 'Die Totale wird hier durch eine Großaufnahme abgelöst' (the wide shot is here replaced by a close-up).
- 'Der Schnitt erfolgt auf Blickachse' (the cut follows the eyeline).

AVOID:
- Anglicisms: 'Der Film featured…' → 'Der Film zeigt…'
- 'The best film of the year' — an absolute claim with no evidence.
- Spoilers: German Filmkritik never reveals the ending.

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: To get under your skin — haunting, deeply affecting; use sparingly in a formal review.
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: The final shot gets under your skin — a silent face held longer than you can bear.

idiom_glosses_en.meaning_en: To set the tone — used in analysis of soundtrack or directorial style.
idiom_glosses_en.example_en: The opening credits already set the tone: a dissonant cello that's never resolved.

lcivic_politische_rede.cultural_notes_en:
POLITICAL SPEECH IN THE GERMAN TRADITION:

(1) BUNDESTAG — the central forum. Unlike the UK (the adversarial Prime Minister's Questions), Bundestag debate is more formal, less interruption-driven, longer. The Regierungserklärung (government declaration) is its own genre.

(2) BRANDT (1913-1992): the Kniefall of 1970 — falling to his knees before the Warsaw Ghetto memorial. Wordless. Deeply divisive in Germany at the time ('he went too far' vs 'it was necessary').

(3) WEIZSÄCKER (1920-2015): the speech for the 40th anniversary of the end of WWII, 8 May 1985. The first time a German president called 8 May a 'Day of Liberation' rather than 'defeat'. A turning point in national memory.

(4) GAUCK (2013-2017): pastor turned president. A moral, sermon-tinged style centred on Freiheit (freedom) and Verantwortung (responsibility). His speeches often opened with a personal anecdote.

(5) MERKEL (2005-2021): the 'sachlich' style — unrhetorical, sparing with metaphor, short sentences, logical chains. 'Wir schaffen das' (2015) — the most contested line of her career.

(6) WHAT'S GERMAN ABOUT IT: German political speech uses less ornamental metaphor than French rhetoric and less religious vocabulary than American oratory. It leans on Sachlichkeit (factual restraint), tight argumentation, and the weight of historical responsibility (historische Verantwortung).
lcivic_politische_rede.tip_advice_en:
ANALYSING A C2 POLITICAL SPEECH:

1. REDESITUATION: Who's speaking? Where? (Bundestag / campaign trail / commemoration) To whom?
2. AUFBAU: Structure — German speeches tend to be very explicit about structure: Einleitung, Hauptteil (three points), Schluss.
3. SPRACHLICHE MITTEL:
- Nominalstil (a marker of Sachlichkeit).
- Passive (offloading agency? 'It was decided' — by whom?).
- Konjunktiv (hedging: 'It would be worth examining whether…').
- Modal verbs (sollen, müssen, dürfen, können — each one maps obligation, possibility, permission differently).
4. SCHLÜSSELWÖRTER: 'Freiheit', 'Verantwortung', 'Gerechtigkeit', 'Sicherheit', 'Europa'.
5. HISTORICAL REFERENCES: German political speech almost always reaches back to NS-Zeit or Wiedervereinigung.

USEFUL PHRASES:
- 'Die Rede inszeniert den Sprecher als…' (the speech stages the speaker as…)
- 'Auffällig ist die Häufung von Passivkonstruktionen — sie…' (the clustering of passive constructions is striking — they…)
- 'Der Konjunktiv II signalisiert hier…' (the subjunctive II here signals…)
lcivic_politische_rede.register_notes_en: C2 GERMAN POLITICAL SPEECH: Nominalstil is the single biggest register marker. 'Die zur Diskussion stehende Frage' beats 'Die Frage, die diskutiert wird'. Passive constructions hide the subject: 'It was decided' (by whom?). Modal verbs sketch obligation: 'müssen' (must), 'sollen' (should — moral), 'dürfen' (be permitted). Konjunktiv I for indirect speech inside the Bundestag: 'The minister said the situation was under control.' Avoid: overblown pathos, colloquialisms, too many Anglicisms.

lcivic_buergerdebatte.cultural_notes_en:
BÜRGERDELIBERATION IN THE GERMAN TRADITION:

(1) HABERMAS (1929-): the theory of Öffentlichkeit (the public sphere) and deliberative democracy. 'The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere' (1962) — a history of public space from the 18th-century bourgeois salon to 20th-century mass media.

(2) THE GERMAN PUBLIC SPHERE: unlike the Anglo-American model, Germany has a strong tradition of Verein (association), Genossenschaft (cooperative), and Mitbestimmung (codetermination in firms — workers on the board). Mediating institutions sit between citizen and state.

(3) STREITKULTUR: since the 1990s Germany has worried about 'Politikverdrossenheit' (political disenchantment). The response: Bürgerdialog, Planungszelle, Bürgerrat — forms of direct or deliberative democracy.

(4) THE MEDIA: public-service broadcasting (ARD, ZDF) has a statutory duty to inform and to provide a forum for debate. A very different model from the US commercial system.

(5) CONTEMPORARY STRESS POINTS: the AfD has broken the post-war consensus (no far right in the Bundestag). Social media fragments the Öffentlichkeit. The open question: does Habermas's model still hold?
lcivic_buergerdebatte.tip_advice_en:
TAKING PART IN A C2 BÜRGERDEBATTE:

1. POSITION BEZIEHEN: 'I'm speaking here as…' — always name the position you're speaking from.
2. ACKNOWLEDGE THE OTHER POSITION: 'I understand your point that…, but…'
3. ATTACK THE ARGUMENT, NOT THE PERSON.
4. EXPOSE YOUR PREMISES: 'My premise is that…' — Germans value transparency about premises.
5. SEEK CONSENSUS, NOT VICTORY: 'Vielleicht können wir uns darauf einigen, dass…' ('Perhaps we can agree that…')

USEFUL PHRASES:
- 'Dem würde ich entgegenhalten, dass…' (I'd counter that…)
- 'Hier liegt, wie mir scheint, ein Missverständnis vor.' (there seems to be a misunderstanding here.)
- 'Lassen Sie uns die Prämissen klären, bevor wir…' (let's clarify the premises before we…)
- 'Das ist ein starkes Argument, allerdings…' (that's a strong argument, but…)

AVOID:
- Ad hominem: 'You don't know what you're talking about!'
- Polemik instead of Argument.
- Silence under provocation — you have to answer, but answer with an argument.
lcivic_buergerdebatte.register_notes_en: C2 BÜRGERDEBATTE: polite but firm. Siezen is mandatory unless you know the person well. Konjunktiv II for politeness: 'Ich würde vorschlagen…' (I'd suggest…), 'Könnten Sie erläutern…' (could you explain…). Don't interrupt — German debate convention is to let the other person finish. When you push back: 'Da muss ich widersprechen' (I have to disagree there) beats 'Das ist Quatsch' (that's nonsense).

idiom_glosses_en.example_en: Let's get to the point — what concrete figures are you basing your forecast on?

lrhet_essay.cultural_notes_en:
THE PHILOSOPHICAL ESSAY — GERMAN TRADITION:

(1) ADORNO (1903-1969): 'The Essay as Form' — the essay is a mode of thought set against the system. It doesn't 'prove' like a treatise (Abhandlung); it 'tries out' like a Versuch.

(2) DIFFERENT FROM THE FRENCH DISSERTATION: a German essay is less rigidly structured, allows 'I' where it earns its place, and can open with an anecdote or a question.

(3) STRUCTURE: an opening (a question or paradox), a body (two or three loops of thought, each going deeper), a close (opening a new question — not shutting it down).

(4) KEY FIGURES: Adorno, Benjamin, Lukács, Arendt, Blumenberg — all wrote philosophical essays.
lrhet_essay.tip_advice_en: Writing a C2 philosophical essay: (1) Open with a real question, not a fake one. (2) Allow yourself to 'think on paper' — write to discover, not to prove what you already know. (3) Use Konjunktiv II for speculation: 'Es könnte sein, dass…' (it could be that…). (4) End openly: 'Vielleicht…' (perhaps…) rather than 'Also…' (so…).

lrhet_kolloquium.cultural_notes_en:
THE GERMAN KOLLOQUIUM / DEFENCE:

(1) Less ritualised than in France: usually 1-2 hours. No 'mention' or honours grade. Just 'bestanden' (passed) or 'nicht bestanden' (failed).

(2) DISPUTATION: a medieval tradition still alive in some departments (especially philosophy). Rigorosum (comprehensive oral exam) vs Disputation (defence of a thesis).

(3) STRATEGY: Germans value Sachlichkeit in the colloquium — no showboating, no defensiveness. Acknowledging a weakness in your work is a sign of strength.
lrhet_kolloquium.tip_advice_en: PREPARING FOR A C2 KOLLOQUIUM: (1) Have three answers ready for 'What's the biggest weakness of your work?' (2) Practise reformulating: 'If I understand you correctly, you mean…' ('Wenn ich Sie richtig verstehe, meinen Sie…'). (3) Use Konjunktiv II for humility: 'There I'd hesitate…' ('Da würde ich zögern…').

lrhet_philosophie.cultural_notes_en:
PHILOSOPHICAL THINKING IN THE GERMAN TRADITION:

(1) KANT (1724-1804): 'Critique of Pure Reason' (1781/1787) — the Copernican revolution in philosophy. Don't ask 'how must our knowledge conform to its objects?' but 'how must objects conform to our knowledge?'. Method: the transcendental deduction.

(2) HEGEL (1770-1831): 'Phenomenology of Spirit' (1807) — thought isn't a static mirror, it's a dialectical motion. Thesis → antithesis → synthesis is the popularised formula; the reality is much messier.

(3) WITTGENSTEIN (1889-1951): wrote in German, global impact. 'Tractatus' (1921): 'What we cannot speak about we must pass over in silence.' 'Philosophical Investigations' (1953): meaning is use (Sprachspiel — language-game).

(4) ADORNO (1903-1969): 'Negative Dialectics' (1966) — against every closed philosophical system. Thought must turn its critique on itself.

(5) WHAT'S GERMAN ABOUT IT: German philosophy is famous for its linguistic difficulty. Kant and Hegel write sentences so long that native speakers have to reread them. But this 'difficulty' is not wilful obscurity — it's the cost of trying to say complex things precisely. A C2 student should read the original, not a translation.
lrhet_philosophie.tip_advice_en:
METHOD FOR A C2 PHILOSOPHY ESSAY:

1. BEGRIFFSANALYSE (concept analysis): define every Begriff (concept) in the question. Distinguish Alltagsbedeutung (everyday meaning) from philosophische Bedeutung (philosophical meaning).

2. EXPOSE THE PRESUPPOSITIONS: every philosophical question carries hidden premises. Your first job is to bring them to light.

3. DEVELOP A THESIS: don't 'answer' the question; propose a thesis and develop it through two or three steps of argument.

4. THINK THROUGH OBJECTIONS: pose the strongest objection to your own position, then answer it.

5. CONCEPTUAL CONSISTENCY: every Begriff is used in exactly one sense throughout the essay.

USEFUL PHRASES:
- 'Es wäre zu fragen, ob…' (one would need to ask whether…)
- 'Unter der Voraussetzung, dass…' (under the premise that…)
- 'Dem ließe sich entgegenhalten, dass…' (one might object that…)
- 'Die entscheidende Unterscheidung ist die zwischen…' (the decisive distinction is between…)

AVOID:
- 'In my opinion…' — philosophy isn't personal opinion.
- 'Humans have always…' — empty generalisation.
- Vague vocabulary: 'irgendwie', 'gewissermaßen', 'eigentlich' (when not strictly needed).

lrhet_persuasion.cultural_notes_en:
PERSUASION THEORY IN THE GERMAN TRADITION:

(1) ARISTOTLE: 'Rhetoric' — three means of persuasion (pisteis): logos, ethos, pathos. Aristotle's claim: ethos is the strongest, because we believe people we respect.

(2) CICERO: 'De oratore' — the ideal orator combines sapientia (knowledge) and eloquentia (eloquence).

(3) PERELMAN (1912-1984): 'The New Rhetoric' (1958, with Olbrechts-Tyteca). Written in French but absorbed into German Rhetorik scholarship. The concept of 'auditoire universel' (the universal audience) is central.

(4) HABERMAS: the theory of the 'ideal speech situation' (herrschaftsfreier Diskurs) — the conditions for rational persuasion: equal participation, only the force of the better argument decides.

(5) GERMAN SCEPTICISM OF RHETORIC: a long tradition of distrust, from Kant ('rhetoric is the art of exploiting human weakness for one's own ends') to Habermas (who distinguishes 'communicative action' from 'strategic action'). But this scepticism is itself a rhetorical stance.

(6) APPLICATIONS: law (Plädoyer — closing argument), politics (Bundestagsrede), business (Pitch). The German register: heavy on facts and figures (logos), suspicious of emotion (pathos), high premium on sincerity (ethos).
lrhet_persuasion.tip_advice_en:
C2 PERSUASION-ANALYSIS GRID:

1. LOGOS: What arguments are made? Facts, statistics, logical inferences? Are there unstated premises (enthymemes)?

2. ETHOS: How does the speaker build credibility? Competence signals, modesty signals, or attacks on the opponent's credibility?

3. PATHOS: Which emotions are appealed to? Fear, hope, indignation, pride? At which point in the text?

4. STRUCTURE: Exordium (opening), Narratio (statement of facts), Argumentatio (proofs), Peroratio (closing appeal).

USEFUL PHRASES:
- 'Die Rede appelliert hier vorwiegend an den logos, indem…' (the speech here appeals mainly to logos by…)
- 'Der ethos des Sprechers wird durch… aufgebaut.' (the speaker's ethos is built up through…)
- 'Der pathos-Appell in der Peroratio zielt darauf ab…' (the pathos appeal in the peroration aims to…)
- 'Diese Konzession ist eine rhetorische Figur, die den ethos stärkt.' (this concession is a rhetorical figure that strengthens ethos.)

larts_medienkritik.cultural_notes_en: MEDIA CRITICISM IN THE GERMAN TRADITION: (1) TRENNUNGSGRUNDSATZ: the separation principle between Nachricht (news) and Kommentar (opinion) — the load-bearing pillar of German journalism. (2) PRESSEKODEX: the German press's code of practice, issued by the Presserat. (3) ÖFFENTLICH-RECHTLICHE: ARD, ZDF — funded by the mandatory broadcasting fee (Rundfunkbeitrag). Their statutory duty: Grundversorgung — basic provision of balanced information. (4) FAZ, SZ, ZEIT, taz, BILD — the German press runs from quality broadsheet to tabloid; the Medienlandschaft (media landscape) is unusually diverse.
larts_medienkritik.tip_advice_en: C2 MEDIA-ANALYSIS GRID: (1) Trennungsgrundsatz: news or opinion? (2) Reporting verbs: 'behaupten' (claim, with doubt) vs 'mitteilen' (state) vs 'einräumen' (concede). (3) Sources: named or anonymous? (4) Agenda-setting: what's reported, what isn't?

lcivic_diplomatie.cultural_notes_en: DIPLOMATIC LANGUAGE: (1) The diplomatic scale (strongest to weakest): verurteilen > bedauern > mit Sorge betrachten > zur Kenntnis nehmen > keinen Kommentar abgeben. (2) Code phrases: 'konstruktiver Meinungsaustausch' = there was no agreement. 'Die Gespräche werden fortgesetzt' = no agreement. (3) Germany as mediator: German diplomacy emphasises 'leise Töne' (quiet tones) and a mediating role.
lcivic_diplomatie.tip_advice_en: SCALE OF DIPLOMATIC VERBS (strong → weak): verurteilen (condemn) > bedauern (regret) > zur Kenntnis nehmen (take note) > nicht kommentieren (no comment). 'Konstruktiver Meinungsaustausch' = disagreement. 'Fortsetzung des Dialogs vereinbart' = no result. ALWAYS: read communiqués twice — once for the public reading, once for the specialist reading.
